item.title: Time's Passage Reveals Layer After Layer of Loss
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Time's Passage Reveals Layer After Layer of Loss

Personal Perspective: With the death of a spouse, you lose more than the person.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • The ways you miss your late spouse both stay the same and change.
  • Along with the person, you miss the structure of marriage--having a helpmate and emotional support.
  • You have to find ways to patch the holes in your life as best you can.
Source: Josue Michel / Unsplash

Last week, as I lifted a heavy laundry basket to carry it to the garage, I thought about how Tom would have carried it for me. I never asked, but if he knew laundry was on my schedule, he’d just do it.

I miss that.

And so much else.

Every year that passes unearths a new stratum in the layers of missing Tom.

I miss his physical presence, his way of thinking, his sense of humor, his creativity, his cooking, his very Tom-ness. There is scarcely a minute of any day when he is not either front and center in my thoughts or lurking in the background.

But six years later, I’m also feeling the loss of having a life mate, a helpmate, a partner, and a supporter in ways that might not occur to anyone who isn’t part of this crappy club.

For example:

Someone to run the household with. The work of maintaining a household—especially one constructed for two people—is endless. Every light bulb that must be changed, every toilet that must be scrubbed, every trash can that must be hauled, every lawn that must be mowed, every quart of milk that must be picked up, every dog that must be walked—is my responsibility. My life feels like an endless chore. I hire help when I can and must, but my income doesn’t go far for that kind of thing. Twice the work, half the budget. I’ve had to lower my standards because a girl can do only so much.

Someone to go out to casual dinners with. Tom and I ate out about once a week, on nights we didn’t feel like cooking. But while I don’t hate eating out alone, it usually doesn’t seem worth the money, and dining out with friends takes a lot more effort than a “let’s eat out tonight” meal with Tom. I've tried very few of the many new restaurants in my neighborhood and can’t remember the last time I went to our favorite spot. I did, however, enjoy a rare impromptu dinner out with a neighbor recently. Note to self: Do that more often.

Someone to gossip with. I do still gossip with friends, but my friends and I don’t all know the same people or see things the same way. I always knew what Tom would want to hear about, and he often had something interesting or hilarious to say about the dish of the day. Especially fun was driving home together after a social event and running the numbers on it—who said what, wore what, did what. Even six years later, when I hear something particularly juicy, my first thought is Wait till I tell Tom!

Someone to cling to at social events. I’m not great in groups. I can be shy, I’m bad at chitchat, and my facial recognition skills are sketchy, so I often don’t recognize people I’ve met before, which is embarrassing. Tom was better at all that—he knew everyone, and everyone knew him—so when I was feeling insecure, which was often, I would stick close to him and ride his personality. Now, out there on my own, I’m more awkward than ever, just a faux pas waiting to happen. My outgoing, bubbly friend Ashley told me about a friend of hers who, when she’s feeling shy and weird, advises herself to “channel your inner Ashley.” I’m not sure I have an inner Ashley, but I may give it a try.

Someone to listen to my insignificant gripes. Traffic was bad. Work was annoying. Someone tailgated me. I had computer problems. Sometimes you just need to vent about the small stuff. I wouldn't inflict such trivial gripes on friends, but I could spew them at Tom. Once, when I was traveling frequently for work, Tom said that he was always glad when I came home because “you have to listen to me.” At the time this annoyed me, but now I totally get it. These days I just do a lot of muttering.

Someone to shop for. Men’s departments make me sad. I loved buying clothes for Tom. (Although he did eventually point out that I kept buying him clothes in the same wine color. What can I say? It looked good on him.) For a long time after my brother, who had schizophrenia, died, I would pick out a present for him every year and donate it to the National Alliance on Mental Illness holiday gift drive. I stopped doing that at some point, but it's time to revive the tradition and find an appropriate nonprofit for a Tom gift as well. Not as good as seeing him wear it, but better than nothing.

Someone to talk me off the ledge. When a friend was unkind, when I inadvertently offended someone, when I had a professional failure, when I embarrassed myself and wanted to crawl under a rock, Tom could always put it in perspective, blow it off for me, or simply reassure me that I was valuable despite my very human flaws. I could tell him things I wouldn’t tell anyone else and trust him to be on my side—whether or not I deserved it. His support was unconditional. Now I have to talk myself down, and I’m not nearly as good at it.

Someone to remember for me. I have an infamously poor memory. I like to say that I’ve had an interesting life; it’s a pity I can’t remember it. Tom and I were together for decades, so much of my life happened with him. When I couldn’t remember something, Tom often could. With his death, I lost many of the stories of my life. On my mind recently: that time when a butcher in England said something that so tickled us, we said it to each other for years after. I wish I could remember what it was. If I ever do, I’ll write it down, as I have many of our inside jokes that I will forget otherwise.

Someone to spoon. Even more than sex, I miss having a warm, solid body to wrap myself around. Physical contact is a basic human need, and skin hunger is real. It used to be that whenever I couldn’t get to sleep, either I would spoon Tom or he would spoon me, and I would drift right off. I sure do miss that. Hugging my 75 lb. dog helps a little, but it’s just not the same.

Nothing is.

item.title: People Get Under Our Skin Because We Open Our Pores to Them
item.description:
Anger

People Get Under Our Skin Because We Open Our Pores to Them

Control anger by using a little ancient wisdom.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Ancient Stoic teachings about managing anger continue to ring true today.
  • Scaling back expectations of others can go a long way to defusing anger.
  • Delay weakens anger’s momentum: Breathe slowly, count backward, or briefly walk away.
Source: PublicDomainPictures/pixabay

Uncontrolled anger can lead to wanton aggression, heated conflict, and a host of negative consequences. But doesn’t anger serve a useful purpose, motivating us to right a wrong, address a grievance, or correct an injustice? Not really.

Whatever useful signal anger may provide in alerting us to a wrong we may have suffered, acting in anger often makes matters worse. Anger doesn’t extinguish fires but only adds fuel to them, clouding our judgment and inciting us to act on impulse regardless of consequences. We don’t need to feel anger to rectify unfairness or respond to an insult. We can act assertively, not aggressively, to remedy situations we perceive as unfair or undeserved, while also keeping our cool.

The Stoic philosophers of ancient times had much to say about anger that still rings true today.

Anger Is a Choice, Not a Reflex

As the Stoic sage Epictetus advised, “If someone succeeds in provoking you, realize that your mind is complicit in the provocation.” It may seem that anger is something that happens to us, not something we make happen. We may say we are overcome by anger, as though it acts on its own accord. But anger is a choice, not a reflex, although it may not be a rational choice.

The human brain is preprogrammed to respond quickly to provocations, all the better in preparing us to either flee or fight off a perceived threat or hostile encounter. We can quickly become “hot under the collar,” but we can also give the thinking brain time to kick in, giving us a chance to analyze and evaluate the situation, to step back and think through our actions before blurting something out—or acting out aggressively.

Let’s say someone bumps into you when getting off a bus and instead of offering an apology, they say, “Hey, get out of the way, jerk.” Outraged, you feel anger rising in the pit of your stomach, which could lead to unfortunate consequences if things get out of hand. Your gut reaction might be to respond with an expletive or perhaps an aggressive gesture involving your middle finger. But you can choose to go in a different direction, letting cooler heads prevail. The buds of anger can be held back from blooming if we exercise our rational brain. It is a choice we make in provocative situations, not an instinctive reaction we are compelled to follow.

Scale Back Your Expectations of Others

They are annoying. They are unfair, even unprincipled. They care only about themselves. They are selfish. They are nasty and inconsiderate. They disappoint you, even when you expect so little from them. They are. . . other people. Yet despite their many flaws, you still interact with them, depend on them, and care about them. As Marcus Aurelius, the 2nd-century Stoic philosopher who also happened to be Emperor of Rome, put it, “When you wake up in the morning, tell yourself: The people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous, and surly... And so none of them can hurt me.” If the Emperor of Rome couldn’t get people to treat him better, who are we to expect anything different from the people we encounter in our daily life?

No One Can Make You Angry Without Your Permission

We open our pores to people when we let their words or actions affect how we feel or invest our self-esteem in their opinions of us. Closing our pores means taking ownership of our own emotions and ways we respond to provocations. You cannot control what others do, but you can control how you respond to them. Anger, like other emotions such as fear, guilt, worry, or disgust, is a private mental experience that no one else can tamper with without our permission.

Don’t let others push your buttons. Suppose someone cheats you in a business deal. You have every right to redress a grievance, to right a wrong, but how you feel about it and what you do about it is up to you. People get under our skin because we open our pores to them. People may treat us badly, but if they succeed in provoking us to anger, it is because we allow them. Marcus advised that when we let go of the belief that we have been injured, we also let go of the feeling of injury. So goes the popular expression, "Don't get mad; get even."

The Stoics believed that things that happen to us don’t determine how we feel; what matters to our emotional well-being is how we interpret them and react to them. Shakespeare voiced this Stoic sentiment when he penned in Hamlet, “... nothing is either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.” When someone treats us badly, we may react in anger if we take it personally and let our emotions boil over. But we can curb a hostile impulse by saying to ourselves that the person did what they thought was right, no matter how misguided they may have been. The bottom line is that while we can’t control what others do, we can control how we react to them. This understanding empowers us to manage our emotional reactions.

Pause to Reflect

Elsewhere on my blog, I focused on suggestions for controlling anger passed down from one of our founding fathers, Thomas Jefferson, who famously advised us that when angry, we should count to 10 before we speak, and if very angry, count to 100.

When you feel yourself becoming angry, delay your response. Delaying techniques are grounded in ancient wisdom, especially that expressed by the Roman Stoic Seneca, who advised pausing because anger loses its momentum when time interrupts it. As Seneca noted, “The greatest remedy for anger is delay.”

Here are some suggestions for putting the delay principle into practice when facing angering situations:

  • Take five slow breaths.
  • Count backwards, slowly, from 10.
  • Say nothing until the emotion subsides.

Tell the other person that you need a moment and walk away before things get out of hand. A simple delay can interrupt impulsive anger. Then, come back with a thoughtful response that takes the other person’s perspective into account, while also expressing your own. You may not reach an agreement, but the other person will likely feel they are being heard.

Laugh It Off

The contemporary Stoic philosopher William Irvine suggests that if you laugh off an insult, it loses its power to make you angry. The situation at hand becomes a problem to be solved, a challenge to face, not a cause for a heated response. Keeping your cool when others get bent out of shape puts you in control—and that makes you stronger.

item.title: How the 'Box Theory' of Dating Hits and Misses
item.description:
Mating

How the 'Box Theory' of Dating Hits and Misses

It could end up boxing you out of dating possibilities.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • According to the "Box Theory," a person will mentally put their date into one of three permanent categories.
  • The categories referred to by "Box Theory" are relationship material, casual sex material, or immaterial.
  • Not everyone uses "Box Theory," and feelings can grow over time—so it's best to remain optimistic.
During a first date, has the other person already put you in some kind of box that you can't get out of no matter what you do?
Source: Israyosoy S. from Pexels

You may have seen this so-called "Box Theory" being mentioned on social media. The theory is that men on a first date with a woman will quickly put the woman into one of three mutually exclusive boxes—relationship material, casual sex material, or essentially immaterial. And that this box supposedly isn't a moving box—meaning that the woman can't do much to move from that box into another.

Is it really this simple then? Do all men do this? Or is the "Box Theory" itself unfairly throwing all men into one, umm, box? Well, on social media channels like Reddit, this theory has certainly caused quite a flap. So, let's unpack this "Box Theory."

What Is This 'Box Theory of Dating'?

A TikToker who goes by the nickname Tinx has asserted in a video post that's gotten over 261K likes that she developed the "Box Theory" to counter the traditional advice that a woman should wait at least three to five dates to sleep with a man so that he is more likely to consider her relationship material. The TikToker argued that the guy will have already boxed the woman sometime early in the first date. “It’s very difficult to shift from box to box, and your behavior doesn’t really affect what box you’re in," says Tinx. "So, if he meets you and he’s like, ‘I wanna date this girl,’ you could puke on his shoes and sleep with him on the first night, and it wouldn’t matter." She continued with, "Vice versa, if he meets you and he just wants to hook up, you could make him wait three months to sleep with you—it’s not gonna change that.”

You certainly can find plenty of men saying similar things about women—that women will also quickly put a man into one of several boxes as well. For example, there's the dreaded friend zone—the she's-never-going-to-sleep-with-you box—that's supposedly as hard to get out of as that Phantom Zone of Superman and Supergirl lore.

There Are Those Who Fit the 'Box Theory'

So are the women claiming that men box women during a first date and the men claiming that women do something similar to men all correct? Well, there are certainly men and women who will, in fact, make rather snap judgments and quickly pigeonhole you when it comes to dating. You'll find people doing that in practically all aspects of life, whether it's in dating, choosing friends, hiring people for a job, deciding on awards or promotions, or even just selecting whom to talk to in a social gathering.

For example, a study published in the journal Psychological Science found that test subjects had already formed judgments about a person's attractiveness, likeability, trustworthiness, competence, and aggressiveness just 100 milliseconds after seeing no more than that person's face. And no one can deny the fact that so many stereotypes and prejudices based solely on appearance continue to exist. It's simply too easy for humans to form firm conclusions about someone without taking the time and effort to really get to know that person.

Therefore, sure, it helps to be aware that such snap judgments can occur. And, yes, investing too much time and effort trying to change the mind of those who have already boxed you in can be like trying to use your forehead only to break open a locked steel box. It may be better instead to move on to other people more open-minded and open to you.

But Not Everyone Fits the 'Box Theory'

Source: cottonbro studio / Pexels

That being said, here's where this "Box Theory" can fall down like a House of Cardboard Boxes—it doesn't apply to all men or all women—or all people, for that matter. There's a tremendous amount of diversity within and across all sexes and genders—ranging from those who will categorize someone in seconds to those who seemingly take forever to decide about anything, with an extensive continuum in between.

Plus, there is the "mere-exposure effect," where people grow to like a person, object, song, idea, haircut, or sweater vest simply because they become more and more familiar with it. This is the basis for a lot of advertising. It's also why like and love can grow between two people over time.

Just look at the variety of "meet cute" stories out there about how long-term couples first met each other. Sure, there's the "We knew it ever since the first time we ever laid eyes on each other in the laundromat" stories. But there are also the "We were just friends for a while before feelings developed" stories, as well as the "We were more bothered by each other at first than hot and bothered" stories. Moreover, various complex factors such as timing and circumstances can play major roles over time.

Signs You've Already Been Boxed

The risk of strictly following the "Box Theory," then, is that you can box your date prematurely as being a boxer when that person hasn't really boxed you at all, prematurely boxing you out of any romantic possibilities with the person in the process. Therefore, it's better instead to stay open-minded until evidence suggests otherwise, such as your date:

  • Making premature assumptions about you. Do they act as if they know you before they, you know, actually know you?
  • Pushing you in a particular direction. For example, if your date mentions the word "sex" over and over again, guess what box you may be in already?
  • Failing to make any effort to get to know you. Do they spend the entire date just talking about themselves or, on the flip side, being about as conversant as Groot?
  • Dissing you or otherwise acting disdainful towards you. "Dis" probably means that you aren't in the relationship material box.
  • Putting other people in boxes, especially permanent ones. If they are quickly making generalities and drawing immovable conclusions about others, then gee, what do you think they might be doing to you?
  • Telling you that you are already in a box. In a variation of what Maya Angelou once said, when someone tells you who they think you are, believe them.

Ultimately, the "Box Theory" might apply to some people but certainly not all. It can oversimplify the true diversity and complexities that exist out there. Your date could very well be an out-of-the-box thinker in more ways than one.

item.title: When a Child’s 'Yes' Is About Survival
item.description:
Trauma

When a Child’s 'Yes' Is About Survival

Liberated children from Oleshky may not be able to choose freely.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • A child’s agreement under threat may be a way to stay safe, not a freely chosen allegiance.
  • Isolation, fear, and repeated messages can shape what children believe about where they belong.
  • The US-Ukraine Foundation has prepared a protocol for ensuring Oleshky's children's uncoerced choice.

There’s some good news coming out of Ukraine, but it’s news with a worrisome psychological aspect. The good news is that “the biggest de-escalation since 2022” is happening in Ukraine now, according to David Arakhamia, head of President Zelensky’s party in Ukraine’s parliament. He was referring to the ceasefire that will allow residents of occupied Oleshky to leave their town and then choose whether to relocate to Russia or within Ukraine. The ceasefire extends until November 1.

For the approximately 2,000 residents of Oleshky, a town in the war zone near Kherson, this means a chance to escape hunger and shelling. Since late spring, the town has been cut off from food deliveries, and the only food that comes is delivered by drones. The roads were heavily mined, and people trying to leave faced death by either landmines or shelling. The humanitarian crisis was acute, and by some accounts, people have resorted to eating grass.

However, as part of the ceasefire agreement, evacuees will first be taken to occupied Crimea or Russia. In the mind of Ukrainian-born American psychotherapist Viktor Dlugunovych, their being sent to Russian-controlled territory is highly problematic.

Russia may say that the departures from Oleshky will be voluntary and residents will be able to choose their destination. However, as Dlugunovych points out, judging from past experience, the ability of the Ukrainians in Russian territory to choose freely is a concern. There’s also the motivation Russia may have to create a propaganda victory by manipulating the evacuees.

Earlier Transfers Are Revealing

Previous experience with Russians and Ukrainians who've been held in captivity provides a reason to look closely at what happens after an initial move to safety. Dlugunovych’s interest is particularly in Ukrainian children and their ability to choose. He doesn’t know firsthand what has been happening in occupied Oleshky since the Russians captured the town in 2022, but as a member of the American-Ukrainian community, he has more than average knowledge of what has happened to Ukrainian children in areas under Russian occupation.

When Agreement Is a Survival Strategy

His concern is, “Children are not small adults. Making sound decisions is absolutely impossible because, anatomically and biologically, when a young mind is threatened, the child will reflexively resort to seeking safety above all. If safety depends on agreeing with Russians, the child will, as a matter of course, agree.”

In occupied areas, at least in previously liberated areas, the inhabitants were cut off from Ukrainian information. The occupiers often told the residents, when they were cut off from information about the outside world, that Russia had already won the war, and that it was Ukraine who had started it.

Added to the problem of disinformation, there’s another factor children are up against. Children, when living under conditions of prolonged stress, will, according to Dlugunovych, experience arrested emotional, intellectual, and social development. “These are signs and symptoms of complex PTSD. If Oreshky is typical of other occupied areas, children will have been forced to speak the Russian language, forced to listen to the Russian National Anthem in school each morning, salute the Russian flag, and be punished if they spoke to each other in Ukrainian.”

He goes on to add, “The complexity of this kind of trauma is immeasurable. You cannot expect children affected by complex PTSD to make wise decisions.”

In his professional experience, the more extreme the propaganda claims, the more they get repeated, and with repetition they may become believed. He cites this example: “A Russian state-television report alleged that Ukrainian soldiers crucified a 3-year-old boy. In the story told on Channel One, the boy and his mother were supposedly targeted because the mother’s husband fought with pro-Russian separatists. The alleged public execution was presented as punishment for that connection and a way to terrorize people who supported the separatists.”

The story was extensively debunked, but according to Dlugunovych, enough Russians believed it that it measurably increased the enlistment rolls in the Russian army.

Listening to Children, Without Pressure

When neutral authorities are judging a child's preference for where he or she lives, listening to them in a pressure-free environment is essential. The Convention on the Rights of the Child requires children’s views to receive due weight according to age and maturity, while making their best interests a primary consideration. UN guidance says those views must be expressed without manipulation, undue influence, or pressure. In Dlugunovych’s mind, the big question is, can these views be expressed when the families are physically in Russia or Russian-occupied territory?

In the case of the Oleshky ceasefire, any de-escalation is welcome. However, the as-yet unanswered question is: Will families, and especially their children, be able to freely choose where they will live, when they are in Russia or occupied territories?

In response to these kinds of concerns, the Washington-based US-Ukraine Foundation asks for the following:

  • No interviews under occupation. No child is asked to choose while under Russian physical or informational control. Any such answer has no evidential weight.
  • An independent humanitarian envoy. Appointed by neither party, with guaranteed, unaccompanied access to the children. The team includes child trauma clinicians, Ukrainian-speaking interviewers, and child-protection officers from a neutral body such as the ICRC or UNICEF.
  • Safe passage to a neutral location. Children travel with independent escorts to a safe third location, not to Russia or a Russian-controlled area.
  • A stabilization and information period. Several weeks of trauma-informed care, accurate information about family and options, and supervised contact with parents or relatives where possible.
  • Family tracing first. Where a parent or legal guardian is identified, reunification with that family is the default.
  • Non-leading interviews. Wishes are ascertained only after stabilization, using evidence-based methods such as the NICHD Protocol (Lamb et al., 2007). Interviews take place out of sight and hearing of anyone linked to the detaining authority.
  • Independent best-interests determination. A panel weighs the child's views alongside family ties, identity, safety, and long-term well-being. Decisions can be reviewed if the child's views change.
  • No media, cameras, or public statements. Children's answers must never become propaganda for either side.

The current ceasefire offers the people of Oleshky a desperately needed chance to escape starvation and shelling. But will it lead to lasting freedom? For children especially, a choice made in fear, isolation, or dependence on those controlling their lives cannot be taken at face value.
